newsitem.title: CANADA: Royal Bank Canada sees strong job growth.
newsitem.headline: Royal Bank Canada sees strong job growth.

text.p: Aggressive interest rate cuts by the Bank of Canada could create more than 400,000 new jobs in the next two years, Royal Bank of Canada said on Wednesday.

"Hundreds of thousands of jobs will be created by the easing of monetary policy that has occurred since October 1995 and, perhaps, by the further easing that could occur over the next several months," Royal Bank's chief economist John McCallum said in a report.
Canada's central bank has chopped rates 16 times in the last 16 months, making short-term loans cheaper in Canada than in the United States, the bank said.
At the same time, deficit-cutting by governments across Canada have assisted in creating the conditions needed for the easing of monetary policy.
These efforts have the set the stage for strong job growth over the next two years, McCallum said. But he acknowledged that Canadians have heard promises of more jobs before.
"Canadians are perhaps getting tired of cliches to the effect that the promised jobs are just around the corner or that there will be light at the end of the tunnel," he said.
But McCallum warned it would be a mistake to reverse the tough fiscal measures imposed by Canadian governments.
"In particular, the core fiscal plan of the federal government remains of central importance," McCallum said.

To calculate the impact on jobs, Royal Bank assumed a 1.0 percent easing of monetary conditions today would cause real gross domestic product (GDP) to rise by 0.4 percent in one year and by 1.0 percent in two years.
The bank then translated the increases in GDP into corresponding improvements in jobs.
Monetary easing to date is forecast to add 255,000 jobs by October 1997 and 315,000 jobs by October 1998, the report said.
The assumed additional easing by the end of this year would add some 40,000 jobs by October 1997 and 90,000 jobs by October 1998, Royal Bank said.
The impact of past monetary easing on jobs in October of this year is relatively small at some 70,000.
"Monetary policy is powerful, but it operates with a lag," McCallum said.
